questions.q: State the diagnostic threshold values for hypertension according to NCERT Class 11 and define systolic and diastolic pressure in one sentence each.
questions.a: Hypertension is diagnosed when repeated blood pressure readings are ≥140/90 mmHg. Systolic pressure (120 mmHg normal) is the peak pressure during ventricular contraction; diastolic pressure (80 mmHg normal) is the minimum pressure during ventricular relaxation. A wrong answer (e.g., 120/80 as hypertension threshold) reveals confusion between normal and pathological values, indicating the student hasn't memorized the clinical cut-off.

questions.q: Explain why hypertension is called a 'silent killer' despite often having no symptoms, using the concept of target organ damage.
questions.a: Hypertension damages organs silently because chronically elevated pressure causes hypertensive arteriolosclerosis (hyaline thickening of arterioles) in kidneys, brain, and retina, leading to nephrosclerosis, lacunar infarcts, and retinopathy before symptoms appear. A wrong answer focusing only on heart failure misses the multi-organ pathophysiology and shows incomplete understanding of systemic vascular damage.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male has BP 150/95 mmHg, LDL 160 mg/dL, HDL 35 mg/dL, and smokes 10 cigarettes/day. Calculate his 10-year cardiovascular risk category using the concept of risk factor clustering and explain which single modifiable factor contributes most to atherosclerotic progression.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify major risk factors — hypertension (stage 1), dyslipidemia (high LDL, low HDL), smoking, male sex, age >45. Step 2: Recognize risk factor clustering multiplies risk synergistically (not additive). Step 3: Smoking causes maximum endothelial dysfunction via oxidative stress, reduced NO bioavailability, and increased platelet adhesiveness. Step 4: Conclude he falls in high-risk category requiring aggressive lifestyle and pharmacotherapy. Wrong answer attributing most risk to LDL alone ignores the multiplicative effect of smoking on plaque rupture.

questions.q: Compare the hemodynamic consequences of chronic hypertension versus acute coronary occlusion on left ventricular workload using the concepts of afterload and preload.
questions.a: Chronic hypertension increases afterload (pressure against which LV must eject), causing concentric hypertrophy (wall thickening) to normalize wall stress (Laplace's law). Acute coronary occlusion reduces contractility → decreased stroke volume → decreased cardiac output → compensatory increased preload (ventricular filling pressure) via Frank-Starling mechanism, leading to pulmonary congestion. Wrong answer confusing afterload/preload changes reveals poor grasp of ventricular-vascular coupling.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Atherosclerosis is solely a lipid storage disease; lowering LDL-cholesterol alone will completely prevent coronary events." Use evidence from plaque biology.
questions.a: The statement is false. Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease: LDL retention initiates but inflammation (macrophages, T-cells, cytokines) drives progression. Plaque stability depends on fibrous cap thickness (collagen synthesis by smooth muscle cells) vs. cap degradation (matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages). Lowering LDL reduces events by ~30% but residual risk persists due to inflammation, thrombosis, and plaque erosion. Wrong agreement shows reductionist view ignoring immuno-metabolic crosstalk.

questions.q: Design a community-based screening protocol for early detection of hypertension and atherosclerotic risk in a rural Indian population, specifying measurement techniques, frequency, and referral criteria.
questions.a: Protocol: 1) Train ASHA workers in automated oscillometric BP measurement (validated device, correct cuff, 3 readings, average last two). 2) Screen all adults ≥30 years annually at village health camps. 3) Refer if BP ≥140/90 on two separate visits OR if BP 130-139/85-89 with diabetes/CKD. 4) Collect fasting lipid profile for referred individuals. 5) Use WHO/ISH risk charts for South Asia to stratify 10-year CVD risk. 6) Refer high-risk (>20%) to PHC for ECG and physician evaluation. Poor answer using only single BP reading or ignoring risk stratification shows lack of public health perspective.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Hypertension is a chronic medical condition ______ by persistently elevated systemic arterial blood pressure (≥140/90 mmHg on repeated measurements) that damages vascular endothelium and target organs.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a 52-year-old ______ office worker who skips breakfast, eats fried snacks at tea-time, and hasn't exercised in years.
What is Hypertension? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Hypertension is a chronic medical condition characterized by persistently elevated systemic arterial blood pressure (≥140/90 mmHg on repeated measurements) that damages vascular endothelium and target organs.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine a ______-year-old Indian office worker who skips breakfast, eats fried snacks at tea-time, and hasn't exercised in years.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can differentiate between primary and secondary hypertension using clinical criteria, explain the stepwise pathogenesis of atherosclerotic plaque formation from endothelial injury to thrombus formation, and correlate ECG changes (ST-segment depression/elevation) with specific coronary artery lesions in a given case study.
